title: Literary Theory post World War II
overview: Is unit mein World War II ke baad ki literary theory aati hai: Structuralism, Deconstruction, Foucault, Lacan, Marxism, Reader-response, Feminism, Postcolonialism, New Historicism, Ecocriticism, Postmodernism, Bakhtin aur Queer theory. NET mein mostly theorist-work matching, famous quotes, coined terms aur chronology ke sawaal aate hain.

topics.title: Structuralism and Narratology: Saussure, Levi-Strauss, Jakobson, Genette
points: Ferdinand de Saussure, Course in General Linguistics (1916): published posthumously by his students Charles Bally and Albert Sechehaye from lecture notes.
Langue (the abstract system of language) vs parole (an individual utterance); structuralism studies langue, not parole.
The sign = signifier (sound-image) + signified (concept); the bond between them is arbitrary (manmana, prakritik nahi).
Meaning arises from difference within the system: 'In language there are only differences without positive terms' (Saussure).
Synchronic (study of language at one moment) vs diachronic (study over time); Saussure privileged the synchronic.
Syntagmatic relations (combination, horizontal) vs paradigmatic/associative relations (selection, vertical).
Claude Levi-Strauss, Structural Anthropology (1958): myths analysed into 'mythemes'; read the Oedipus myth through binary oppositions.

Roman Jakobson: 'Two Aspects of Language' (1956) opposes metaphor (selection/similarity) and metonymy (combination/contiguity); 'Linguistics and Poetics' (1960) gives six functions of language, incl. the poetic function.
Vladimir Propp, Morphology of the Folktale (1928, English 1958): 31 functions and 7 spheres of action (villain, donor, helper, princess, dispatcher, hero, false hero).
A. J. Greimas, Structural Semantics (1966): six actants; Tzvetan Todorov coined 'narratology' (Grammaire du Decameron, 1969).
Gerard Genette, Narrative Discourse (Figures III, 1972): order, duration, frequency, mood, voice; introduced 'focalization'; homodiegetic/heterodiegetic narrators.
Jonathan Culler, Structuralist Poetics (1975): 'literary competence', the reader's internalised grammar of literary conventions.

topics.title: Roland Barthes: from structuralism to post-structuralism
points: Roland Barthes, Mythologies (1957): myth as second-order semiological system (the Black soldier saluting the French flag on Paris-Match).
'The Death of the Author' (1967 in English in Aspen; French 1968): 'the birth of the reader must be at the cost of the death of the Author'.
Barthes: a text is 'a tissue of quotations drawn from the innumerable centres of culture'; the author is replaced by the 'scriptor'.
S/Z (1970): a lexia-by-lexia reading of Balzac's novella Sarrasine using five codes.
The five codes of S/Z: hermeneutic, proairetic (action), semic, symbolic and cultural (referential).
S/Z distinguishes the readerly (lisible) text, consumed passively, from the writerly (scriptible) text, produced by the reader.
'From Work to Text' (1971): the work is held in the hand, the text is held in language; text is plural and a methodological field.
The Pleasure of the Text (1973): plaisir (comfortable pleasure) vs jouissance (disruptive bliss).
Camera Lucida (1980): studium vs punctum in photography; A Lover's Discourse (1977); Elements of Semiology (1964).

topics.title: Post-structuralism and Deconstruction: Jacques Derrida
points: Derrida's paper 'Structure, Sign and Play in the Discourse of the Human Sciences' was read at Johns Hopkins University in October 1966; it is taken as the birth of post-structuralism in America.
In 1967 Derrida published three books: Of Grammatology, Writing and Difference, and Speech and Phenomena.
Of Grammatology was translated into English by Gayatri Chakravorty Spivak in 1976, with a long translator's preface.
'There is nothing outside the text' (il n'y a pas de hors-texte) comes from Of Grammatology, in the reading of Rousseau.
Logocentrism: Western metaphysics' longing for a 'transcendental signified' or 'metaphysics of presence'; phonocentrism privileges speech over writing.
Differance (with an 'a'): meaning both differs and is endlessly deferred; the 'a' is audible only in writing.
Key concepts: trace, supplement (Rousseau), aporia, decentring, free play, sous rature (under erasure, borrowed from Heidegger), pharmakon (in 'Plato's Pharmacy', Dissemination, 1972).
Deconstruction reverses and displaces violent binary hierarchies (speech/writing, presence/absence, man/woman).
Later works: Dissemination (1972), Margins of Philosophy (1972), Glas (1974), Spectres of Marx (1993), The Gift of Death (1992).
Yale School: Paul de Man (Blindness and Insight 1971, Allegories of Reading 1979), J. Hillis Miller, Geoffrey Hartman, Harold Bloom; collective volume Deconstruction and Criticism (1979).
J. Hillis Miller, 'The Critic as Host' (1977); Barbara Johnson, The Critical Difference (1980); Christopher Norris, Deconstruction: Theory and Practice (1982).

topics.title: Michel Foucault: discourse, power, knowledge
points: Major works: Madness and Civilization (Histoire de la folie, 1961), The Birth of the Clinic (1963), The Order of Things (1966), The Archaeology of Knowledge (1969).
Discipline and Punish: The Birth of the Prison (1975): uses Jeremy Bentham's Panopticon as a model of disciplinary surveillance.
The History of Sexuality, Vol. 1: The Will to Knowledge (1976): rejects the 'repressive hypothesis'; sexuality is produced by discourse; introduces biopower.
Episteme: the underlying grid of knowledge of an age (Renaissance, Classical, Modern), set out in The Order of Things.
The Order of Things ends with the claim that 'man' is a recent invention who may be 'erased, like a face drawn in sand at the edge of the sea'.
Power is not merely repressive but productive and everywhere; 'power/knowledge' are inseparable (Power/Knowledge, 1980, ed. Colin Gordon).
'What Is an Author?' (lecture 1969): the 'author-function' as a discursive classification; ends asking 'What difference does it make who is speaking?'
Methods: archaeology (early) and genealogy (later, from Nietzsche: 'Nietzsche, Genealogy, History', 1971).
Foucault strongly influenced New Historicism (Greenblatt), Said's Orientalism and queer theory.

topics.title: Psychoanalytic criticism: Freud, Jung, Bloom
points: Sigmund Freud, The Interpretation of Dreams (1899, dated 1900): the dream-work operates through condensation, displacement, considerations of representability and secondary revision.
Freud's topography: id, ego, superego (The Ego and the Id, 1923); Oedipus complex; 'Creative Writers and Day-Dreaming' (1908).
Freud, 'The Uncanny' (Das Unheimliche, 1919) reads E. T. A. Hoffmann's 'The Sandman'; Beyond the Pleasure Principle (1920) introduces the death drive and the fort-da game.
Ernest Jones, Hamlet and Oedipus (1949): Hamlet's delay explained by the Oedipus complex.
Carl Jung: collective unconscious and archetypes (shadow, anima/animus, persona); basis of myth/archetypal criticism (Northrop Frye, Anatomy of Criticism, 1957).
Harold Bloom, The Anxiety of Influence (1973): the 'strong poet' misreads (misprision) a precursor; six revisionary ratios: clinamen, tessera, kenosis, daemonization, askesis, apophrades.
Bloom, A Map of Misreading (1975); The Western Canon (1994).
Norman Holland, The Dynamics of Literary Response (1968) and 5 Readers Reading (1975): psychoanalytic reader-response, 'identity theme'.
Peter Brooks, Reading for the Plot (1984); Shoshana Felman on The Turn of the Screw; Slavoj Zizek popularises Lacan through popular culture.

topics.title: Jacques Lacan
points: Lacan's call was a 'return to Freud' read through Saussurean linguistics; his collected papers are Ecrits (1966).
'The unconscious is structured like a language' (Lacan); metaphor corresponds to condensation and metonymy to displacement.
The mirror stage (paper 1936, revised 1949): an infant of about 6-18 months misrecognises (meconnaissance) itself as a unified whole in the mirror; origin of the ego.
Three orders: the Imaginary, the Symbolic and the Real.
Entry into the Symbolic order is governed by the Name-of-the-Father (nom du pere); the phallus is the privileged signifier.
Lacan inverts Saussure's sign: the signifier (S) over the signified (s), with a 'bar' resisting signification; signifiers 'slide' over signifieds.
'Man's desire is the desire of the Other' (Lacan); objet petit a is the unattainable object-cause of desire.
'Seminar on The Purloined Letter' (1956, opens Ecrits) reads Poe's tale as the movement of the signifier; Derrida replied in 'The Purveyor of Truth' (1975).
Lacan's work underlies the French feminists (Kristeva, Irigaray, Cixous) and film theory (Laura Mulvey, 'Visual Pleasure and Narrative Cinema', 1975, 'the male gaze').

topics.title: Marxist criticism: Althusser, Macherey, Williams and the Frankfurt School
points: Base and superstructure: the economic base determines the cultural superstructure (Marx, Preface to A Contribution to the Critique of Political Economy, 1859).

Louis Althusser, 'Ideology and Ideological State Apparatuses' (1970): ideology 'interpellates' (hails) individuals as subjects; Repressive State Apparatus vs Ideological State Apparatuses (school, church, family, media).
Althusser: ideology represents 'the imaginary relationship of individuals to their real conditions of existence'.
Pierre Macherey, A Theory of Literary Production (1966): a text is produced, not created; read its 'silences' and gaps, the 'not-said'.
Georg Lukacs: The Theory of the Novel (1916, book 1920), The Historical Novel (1937), favoured critical realism and 'typicality'; opposed modernist experimentalism.
Antonio Gramsci, Prison Notebooks (written 1929-35): 'hegemony', rule by consent; also the term 'subaltern'.

Raymond Williams: Culture and Society (1958), The Long Revolution (1961), The Country and the City (1973), Keywords (1976), Marxism and Literature (1977): 'structure of feeling'; dominant, residual and emergent culture; 'culture is ordinary' (1958).

Frankfurt School: Adorno and Horkheimer, Dialectic of Enlightenment (1944/1947), 'the culture industry'; Walter Benjamin, 'The Work of Art in the Age of Mechanical Reproduction' (1935/36), loss of 'aura'.
Birmingham Centre for Contemporary Cultural Studies founded 1964 by Richard Hoggart (The Uses of Literacy, 1957); Stuart Hall, 'Encoding/Decoding' (1973).

topics.title: Marxist criticism: Terry Eagleton and Fredric Jameson
points: Terry Eagleton: Criticism and Ideology (1976), Marxism and Literary Criticism (1976), Literary Theory: An Introduction (1983), The Function of Criticism (1984), The Ideology of the Aesthetic (1990), After Theory (2003).
Eagleton's Literary Theory: An Introduction (1983) argues literature has no essence and is defined by value-judgements; ends with 'Political Criticism'.
Eagleton, Criticism and Ideology: categories such as General Mode of Production, Literary Mode of Production, General Ideology, Authorial Ideology, Aesthetic Ideology.
Fredric Jameson: Marxism and Form (1971), The Prison-House of Language (1972, on structuralism and Russian Formalism).
Jameson, The Political Unconscious: Narrative as a Socially Symbolic Act (1981): opens with the slogan 'Always historicize!'
The Political Unconscious proposes three concentric horizons of interpretation: political history, society (class discourse/ideologeme), and history as modes of production.
Jameson, 'Postmodernism, or, The Cultural Logic of Late Capitalism' (New Left Review, 1984; book 1991): pastiche as 'blank parody', waning of affect, depthlessness, 'cognitive mapping'.
Jameson, 'Third-World Literature in the Era of Multinational Capital' (1986): third-world texts as 'national allegories'; answered by Aijaz Ahmad, In Theory (1992).

topics.title: Reader-response and Reception theory
points: Reader-response shifts attention from text and author to the reader; it rejects the New Critical 'Affective Fallacy' (Wimsatt and Beardsley, 1949).
Louise Rosenblatt: Literature as Exploration (1938) and The Reader, the Text, the Poem (1978): 'transactional' theory, efferent vs aesthetic reading.
Wolfgang Iser (Konstanz School): The Implied Reader (1972, Eng. 1974) and The Act of Reading (1976, Eng. 1978): gaps or blanks, indeterminacy, 'wandering viewpoint', the 'implied reader'.
Hans Robert Jauss: 'Literary History as a Challenge to Literary Theory' (1967, Konstanz inaugural lecture): 'horizon of expectations' (Erwartungshorizont); 'aesthetic distance'.
Jauss builds on Hans-Georg Gadamer, Truth and Method (1960): 'fusion of horizons'.
Stanley Fish: Surprised by Sin: The Reader in Paradise Lost (1967); 'Literature in the Reader: Affective Stylistics' (1970); Self-Consuming Artifacts (1972).
Fish, Is There a Text in This Class? The Authority of Interpretive Communities (1980): meaning is produced by 'interpretive communities'.
Umberto Eco, The Role of the Reader (1979): open vs closed texts, 'model reader'; The Open Work (1962).
David Bleich, Subjective Criticism (1978); Norman Holland's 'identity theme'; Gerald Prince coined 'narratee' (1973); Judith Fetterley's 'resisting reader' (1978).
Wayne Booth, The Rhetoric of Fiction (1961) coined 'implied author'; Iser's implied reader is its counterpart.

topics.title: Feminist criticism: Beauvoir, Showalter, Gilbert and Gubar
points: Simone de Beauvoir, The Second Sex (1949): 'One is not born, but rather becomes, a woman'; woman as the 'Other' to man as Subject.
Precursors: Mary Wollstonecraft, A Vindication of the Rights of Woman (1792); Virginia Woolf, A Room of One's Own (1929, 'a woman must have money and a room of her own') and Three Guineas (1938).
Betty Friedan, The Feminine Mystique (1963); Kate Millett, Sexual Politics (1970) attacks Lawrence, Henry Miller, Norman Mailer and Jean Genet.
Elaine Showalter, A Literature of Their Own (1977): three phases of women's writing: Feminine (1840-1880), Feminist (1880-1920), Female (1920 onwards).
Showalter, 'Towards a Feminist Poetics' (1979) coined 'gynocritics/gynocriticism' (woman as writer) as distinct from 'feminist critique' (woman as reader).
Showalter, 'Feminist Criticism in the Wilderness' (1981): four models of difference: biological, linguistic, psychoanalytic and cultural.
Sandra Gilbert and Susan Gubar, The Madwoman in the Attic: The Woman Writer and the Nineteenth-Century Literary Imagination (1979); title from Bertha Mason in Jane Eyre.
Gilbert and Gubar: images of 'angel' and 'monster'; the woman writer's 'anxiety of authorship' (revising Bloom's 'anxiety of influence'); they opened with 'Is a pen a metaphorical penis?'
Gilbert and Gubar edited The Norton Anthology of Literature by Women (1985).

Others: Ellen Moers, Literary Women (1976); Adrienne Rich, 'When We Dead Awaken: Writing as Re-Vision' (1971) and 'Compulsory Heterosexuality and Lesbian Existence' (1980); Toril Moi, Sexual/Textual Politics (1985).
Alice Walker, In Search of Our Mothers' Gardens (1983) defines 'womanism'; bell hooks, Ain't I a Woman (1981); Chandra Talpade Mohanty, 'Under Western Eyes' (1984).

topics.title: French feminism and Judith Butler
points: Helene Cixous, 'The Laugh of the Medusa' (1975): 'Woman must write her self'; coined 'ecriture feminine' (feminine writing), writing 'in white ink'.
Cixous and Catherine Clement, The Newly Born Woman (1975), containing 'Sorties', which lists patriarchal binaries (activity/passivity, sun/moon, culture/nature, man/woman).

Julia Kristeva: coined 'intertextuality' in 'Word, Dialogue and Novel' (1966/67), drawing on Bakhtin; Revolution in Poetic Language (1974): the semiotic vs the symbolic; the 'chora' (from Plato's Timaeus).
Kristeva, Powers of Horror: An Essay on Abjection (1980); Desire in Language (1980); 'Women's Time' (1979).
Luce Irigaray: Speculum of the Other Woman (1974), which got her expelled from Lacan's Ecole freudienne; This Sex Which Is Not One (1977).
Irigaray proposes 'parler-femme' (speaking as woman) and strategic 'mimicry' of patriarchal discourse; female sexuality as plural.
Judith Butler, Gender Trouble: Feminism and the Subversion of Identity (1990): gender is 'performative', 'the repeated stylization of the body'; drag exposes gender as imitation.
Butler: Bodies That Matter (1993), Excitable Speech (1997), Undoing Gender (2004); she draws on Foucault, Derrida, Austin's speech-act theory and Beauvoir.
Monique Wittig, 'One Is Not Born a Woman' (1981) and The Straight Mind (1992): the lesbian is not a 'woman'.

topics.title: Postcolonialism: Said, Spivak, Bhabha
points: Edward Said, Orientalism (1978): the Orient as a European construction; Orientalism as a Western style 'for dominating, restructuring, and having authority over the Orient'; draws on Foucault and Gramsci.
Said, Culture and Imperialism (1993): 'contrapuntal reading'; reads Jane Austen's Mansfield Park (Antigua plantation), Kipling's Kim, Camus, Conrad.
Said's other works: The Question of Palestine (1979), Covering Islam (1981), The World, the Text, and the Critic (1983), Representations of the Intellectual (1994), Out of Place (memoir, 1999).
Gayatri Chakravorty Spivak, 'Can the Subaltern Speak?' (1985 in Wedge; expanded 1988 in Marxism and the Interpretation of Culture, eds. Nelson and Grossberg): concludes 'the subaltern cannot speak'.
In that essay Spivak analyses sati and the formula 'White men are saving brown women from brown men'; she critiques Foucault and Deleuze; 'epistemic violence'.

Spivak: 'Three Women's Texts and a Critique of Imperialism' (1985, on Jane Eyre, Wide Sargasso Sea and Frankenstein); In Other Worlds (1987); A Critique of Postcolonial Reason (1999); 'strategic essentialism'.
Homi K. Bhabha, The Location of Culture (1994); edited Nation and Narration (1990).
Bhabha, 'Of Mimicry and Man' (1984): colonial mimicry produces a subject 'almost the same, but not quite' (and 'almost the same but not white'); cites Macaulay's Minute (1835).
Bhabha's key concepts: hybridity, ambivalence, mimicry, 'Third Space' of enunciation, 'unhomely'; 'Signs Taken for Wonders' (1985).
Said, Spivak and Bhabha are called the 'Holy Trinity' of postcolonial theory (Robert Young).

topics.title: Postcolonialism: Fanon, Ngugi and others
points: Frantz Fanon (Martinique, worked in Algeria): Black Skin, White Masks (1952) on the psychology of colonial racism; 'Look, a Negro!'
Fanon, The Wretched of the Earth (1961), with a preface by Jean-Paul Sartre; defends anti-colonial violence; includes 'On National Culture' and the pitfalls of national consciousness.
Fanon's three phases of the native intellectual: assimilation, remembering/return to the past, and the fighting (revolutionary) phase.
Ngugi wa Thiong'o, Decolonising the Mind: The Politics of Language in African Literature (1986): bids farewell to English and commits to Gikuyu; 'language as culture'.
Ngugi, Owuor-Anyumba and Taban Lo Liyong, 'On the Abolition of the English Department' (1968, Nairobi).
Ngugi's novels: Weep Not, Child (1964), The River Between (1965), A Grain of Wheat (1967), Petals of Blood (1977), Devil on the Cross (in Gikuyu, 1980); Moving the Centre (1993).
Chinua Achebe, 'An Image of Africa: Racism in Conrad's Heart of Darkness' (lecture 1975): called Conrad 'a thoroughgoing racist' (earlier 'bloody racist').
Aime Cesaire, Discourse on Colonialism (1950); Negritude movement of Cesaire, Leopold Senghor and Leon Damas (1930s).
Ashcroft, Griffiths and Tiffin, The Empire Writes Back (1989): 'abrogation' and 'appropriation' of English; 'english' vs 'English'.

Others: Ranajit Guha and Subaltern Studies (from 1982); Benedict Anderson, Imagined Communities (1983); Aijaz Ahmad, In Theory (1992); Robert Young, White Mythologies (1990) and Colonial Desire (1995).

topics.title: New Historicism and Cultural Materialism
points: Stephen Greenblatt coined 'New Historicism' in 1982 (introduction to a special issue of Genre on Renaissance forms of power); he later preferred 'cultural poetics' ('Towards a Poetics of Culture', 1987).
Greenblatt, Renaissance Self-Fashioning: From More to Shakespeare (1980): identity is fashioned within power structures.
Greenblatt, 'Invisible Bullets' (1981, on Thomas Harriot and Henry IV): the 'subversion-containment' model, authority produces subversion in order to contain it.
Greenblatt, Shakespearean Negotiations (1988): 'social energy', 'circulation', 'negotiation', 'exchange'; Will in the World (2004); The Swerve (2011).
Louis Montrose's formula: 'the historicity of texts and the textuality of history'.

New Historicism reads literary and non-literary texts side by side ('parallel reading'), often beginning with an anecdote; it draws on Foucault and Clifford Geertz's 'thick description' (The Interpretation of Cultures, 1973).
Hayden White, Metahistory (1973): history as narrative emplotment (romance, tragedy, comedy, satire).
Cultural Materialism (British): the term comes from Raymond Williams; key text Political Shakespeare (1985), eds. Jonathan Dollimore and Alan Sinfield.
Political Shakespeare's foreword names four features: historical context, theoretical method, political commitment and textual analysis.
Jonathan Dollimore, Radical Tragedy: Religion, Ideology and Power in the Drama of Shakespeare and His Contemporaries (1984); Sexual Dissidence (1991); Alan Sinfield, Faultlines (1992).
Difference: New Historicism (American) stresses containment; Cultural Materialism (British, Marxist) stresses dissidence and present-day political use of texts.

topics.title: Ecocriticism
points: The term 'ecocriticism' was coined by William Rueckert in 'Literature and Ecology: An Experiment in Ecocriticism' (1978).
Cheryll Glotfelty and Harold Fromm (eds), The Ecocriticism Reader (1996): 'ecocriticism is the study of the relationship between literature and the physical environment'.
ASLE (Association for the Study of Literature and Environment) founded 1992; its journal ISLE began 1993.
Joseph Meeker, The Comedy of Survival (1972) coined 'literary ecology'; Rachel Carson, Silent Spring (1962) is a founding environmental text.
Lawrence Buell, The Environmental Imagination (1995) on Thoreau; The Future of Environmental Criticism (2005) describes first-wave and second-wave ecocriticism.
Jonathan Bate, Romantic Ecology: Wordsworth and the Environmental Tradition (1991) and The Song of the Earth (2000): British 'green studies'.
Greg Garrard, Ecocriticism (2004, New Critical Idiom): pollution, wilderness, apocalypse, dwelling, animals, the earth.
Arne Naess coined 'deep ecology' (1973); Francoise d'Eaubonne coined 'ecofeminism' (1974).
Timothy Morton, Ecology without Nature (2007), 'dark ecology', Hyperobjects (2013); Rob Nixon, Slow Violence and the Environmentalism of the Poor (2011).
Amitav Ghosh, The Great Derangement: Climate Change and the Unthinkable (2016); Leo Marx, The Machine in the Garden (1964); Raymond Williams, The Country and the City (1973).

topics.title: Postmodernism: Lyotard, Baudrillard, Hutcheon
points: Jean-Francois Lyotard, The Postmodern Condition: A Report on Knowledge (1979; English 1984, foreword by Jameson), written for the Quebec government.
Lyotard: 'I define postmodern as incredulity toward metanarratives'; prefers 'petits recits' (little narratives), language games (Wittgenstein) and 'paralogy'.
Jean Baudrillard, Simulacra and Simulation (1981): simulacrum, 'hyperreality', 'the precession of simulacra'; the map precedes the territory (Borges fable).
Baudrillard's four phases of the image: reflects a basic reality, masks and perverts it, masks its absence, and finally bears no relation to any reality (pure simulacrum).
Baudrillard: Disneyland is presented as imaginary to make us believe the rest of America is real; The Gulf War Did Not Take Place (1991).
Linda Hutcheon, A Poetics of Postmodernism (1988) coined 'historiographic metafiction'; The Politics of Postmodernism (1989); Narcissistic Narrative (1980); A Theory of Parody (1985).
Historiographic metafiction examples: Fowles's The French Lieutenant's Woman, Rushdie's Midnight's Children, Doctorow's Ragtime.
Ihab Hassan, The Dismemberment of Orpheus (1971) and his table of modernism vs postmodernism; Brian McHale, Postmodernist Fiction (1987): the 'ontological dominant'.
Jurgen Habermas, 'Modernity: An Incomplete Project' (1980) defends modernity against postmodernism.
John Barth, 'The Literature of Exhaustion' (1967) and 'The Literature of Replenishment' (1980); Patricia Waugh, Metafiction (1984); Deleuze and Guattari, A Thousand Plateaus (1980): the 'rhizome'.

topics.title: Mikhail Bakhtin and the Bakhtin Circle
points: Problems of Dostoevsky's Art (1929), revised as Problems of Dostoevsky's Poetics (1963): the 'polyphonic' novel of independent, unmerged voices.
Rabelais and His World (written as a 1940 dissertation, published 1965): 'carnivalesque', 'grotesque realism', the grotesque body, folk laughter.
The Dialogic Imagination (four essays, Russian 1975; English 1981, ed. Michael Holquist, trans. Caryl Emerson and Holquist) includes 'Epic and Novel' and 'Discourse in the Novel'.
'Discourse in the Novel' (1934-35): 'heteroglossia' (raznorechie), the novel as an orchestration of social languages; centripetal vs centrifugal forces of language.
'Forms of Time and of the Chronotope in the Novel' (1937-38): 'chronotope', the intrinsic connectedness of time and space in literature.
Dialogism: every utterance responds to earlier ones and anticipates replies; opposed to the monologic (epic, Tolstoy in Bakhtin's view).
'Epic and Novel': the epic belongs to an 'absolute past', the novel is the genre of becoming and contact with the open-ended present.
Bakhtin Circle: V. N. Voloshinov, Marxism and the Philosophy of Language (1929); P. N. Medvedev, The Formal Method in Literary Scholarship (1928); authorship of these is disputed.
Speech Genres and Other Late Essays (English 1986); Kristeva introduced Bakhtin to the West and derived 'intertextuality' from his dialogism.

topics.title: Queer theory
points: The term 'queer theory' was coined by Teresa de Lauretis at a 1990 conference, published in a special issue of differences (1991).
Eve Kosofsky Sedgwick, Between Men: English Literature and Male Homosocial Desire (1985): 'homosocial desire', erotic triangles (after Rene Girard).
Sedgwick, Epistemology of the Closet (1990): the homo/heterosexual definition structures modern Western culture; Axiom 1: 'People are different from each other'.
Judith Butler, Gender Trouble (1990) and Bodies That Matter (1993): gender performativity is foundational to queer theory.
Foucault, History of Sexuality Vol. 1 (1976): 'The sodomite had been a temporary aberration; the homosexual was now a species'.
Michael Warner popularised 'heteronormativity' (Fear of a Queer Planet, 1991/1993); Adrienne Rich, 'compulsory heterosexuality' (1980).
Gayle Rubin, 'The Traffic in Women' (1975, 'sex/gender system') and 'Thinking Sex' (1984); Diana Fuss (ed.), Inside/Out (1991).

Later queer theory: Lee Edelman, No Future: Queer Theory and the Death Drive (2004, 'reproductive futurism'); Jack Halberstam, Female Masculinity (1998); Jose Esteban Munoz, Cruising Utopia (2009); Jasbir Puar, Terrorist Assemblages (2007, 'homonationalism').
Queer reading of canon: Sedgwick on Henry James's 'The Beast in the Jungle'; Alan Sinfield, The Wilde Century (1994).

terms.hindi: भाषा की पूरी व्यवस्था या नियम जो सब बोलने वालों में साझा हैं।
terms.net: Saussure's term (Course in General Linguistics, 1916) for the abstract, collective system of rules and conventions of a language, as opposed to parole.

terms.hindi: किसी व्यक्ति का असली बोला या लिखा हुआ वाक्य।
terms.net: Saussure's term for the individual, concrete act of speech or utterance drawn from the system of langue.

terms.hindi: शब्द की आवाज़ या लिखा रूप, जैसे 'पेड़' शब्द।
terms.net: In Saussure, the material component of the linguistic sign, the sound-image or written mark, joined arbitrarily to a signified.

terms.hindi: शब्द सुनकर मन में आने वाला विचार या अर्थ।
terms.net: In Saussure, the conceptual component of the sign, the mental concept evoked by the signifier.

terms.hindi: दो उल्टे जोड़े, जैसे दिन-रात, पुरुष-स्त्री।
terms.net: A pair of opposed terms (nature/culture, speech/writing) through which, for Levi-Strauss and structuralists, meaning is organised; deconstruction exposes their hierarchy.

terms.hindi: मिथक (कथा) की सबसे छोटी अर्थपूर्ण इकाई।
terms.net: Levi-Strauss's term (Structural Anthropology, 1958) for the minimal constituent unit of a myth, analogous to the phoneme in language.

terms.hindi: कहानी कहने की बनावट का शास्त्र।
terms.net: The structuralist science of narrative structure; term coined by Tzvetan Todorov (Grammaire du Decameron, 1969); developed by Genette, Greimas, Bal.

terms.hindi: कहानी किसकी नज़र से देखी जा रही है।
terms.net: Genette's term (Narrative Discourse, 1972) for the perspective through which narrated events are perceived (zero, internal, external), distinct from the narrating voice.

terms.hindi: ऐसा पाठ जिसमें पाठक खुद अर्थ बनाता है।
terms.net: Barthes's 'scriptible' text (S/Z, 1970), which makes the reader an active producer of meaning, opposed to the 'readerly' (lisible) text consumed passively.

terms.hindi: गहरा, बेचैन कर देने वाला आनंद।
terms.net: Barthes (The Pleasure of the Text, 1973): blissful, disruptive pleasure that unsettles the reader's cultural assumptions, opposed to plaisir; also used by Lacan and Cixous.

terms.hindi: यह मान्यता कि कोई अंतिम, पक्का केंद्र या सत्य है।
terms.net: Derrida's term for Western metaphysics' reliance on a 'transcendental signified' or presence (God, reason, origin) that would ground meaning outside the play of signs.

terms.hindi: अर्थ हमेशा फ़र्क से बनता है और आगे टलता रहता है।
terms.net: Derrida's coinage combining French 'to differ' and 'to defer': meaning arises from difference and is perpetually postponed; the 'a' is visible only in writing.

terms.hindi: ऐसी उलझन जिसका कोई हल न निकले।
terms.net: Greek 'impasse'; in deconstruction (Derrida, de Man) an undecidable point where a text's logic contradicts itself and meaning cannot be resolved.

terms.hindi: शब्द को काटकर भी लिखा रहने देना।
terms.net: 'Under erasure': Derrida's practice, from Heidegger, of writing a word and crossing it out, since it is inadequate yet necessary.

terms.hindi: किसी युग की सोच का छिपा ढाँचा।
terms.net: Foucault (The Order of Things, 1966): the underlying configuration of knowledge that determines what can be thought and said in a given epoch.

terms.hindi: किसी विषय पर बोलने-सोचने का तय तरीका जो सत्ता से जुड़ा है।
terms.net: In Foucault, a historically specific system of statements and practices that produces knowledge and its objects and is inseparable from power.

terms.hindi: ऐसी जेल जहाँ हर कैदी को लगे कि उसे हमेशा देखा जा रहा है।
terms.net: Jeremy Bentham's prison design, used by Foucault in Discipline and Punish (1975) as the model of disciplinary power through constant visibility and self-surveillance.

terms.hindi: बच्चा शीशे में खुद को पहली बार पूरा देखकर 'मैं' बनाता है।
terms.net: Lacan's concept (1936; 1949 paper in Ecrits): the infant's misrecognition of its unified reflection, founding the ego in the Imaginary order.

terms.hindi: जानी-पहचानी चीज़ जो अचानक डरावनी लगे।
terms.net: Freud's 'Das Unheimliche' (1919): the frightening that leads back to the familiar, the return of the repressed; illustrated through Hoffmann's 'The Sandman'.

terms.hindi: समाज की विचारधारा का हमें 'पुकार' कर एक पहचान दे देना।
terms.net: Althusser ('Ideology and Ideological State Apparatuses', 1970): the process by which ideology 'hails' individuals and constitutes them as subjects.

terms.hindi: स्कूल, धर्म, परिवार जैसे संस्थान जो सोच गढ़ते हैं।
terms.net: Althusser's term for institutions (school, church, family, media, culture) that secure domination by ideology, as distinct from the Repressive State Apparatus (police, army).

terms.hindi: ज़बरदस्ती नहीं, सहमति से चलने वाला प्रभुत्व।
terms.net: Gramsci (Prison Notebooks): domination of a ruling class achieved through cultural consent rather than force alone.

terms.hindi: किसी दौर का साझा अनुभव और भावनाओं का माहौल।
terms.net: Raymond Williams (The Long Revolution 1961; Marxism and Literature 1977): the lived, emergent experience of a period, felt before it is fully articulated.

terms.hindi: किसी समय के पाठकों की पहले से बनी उम्मीदें।
terms.net: Jauss (1967): the set of cultural and literary norms and assumptions against which readers of a given period receive and judge a work.

terms.hindi: वह पाठक जिसकी कल्पना पाठ खुद करता है।
terms.net: Iser (The Implied Reader, 1972): the reader role inscribed in the text's structure, who fills its gaps; parallels Booth's 'implied author'.

terms.hindi: पाठकों का समूह जो एक जैसे नियमों से अर्थ निकालता है।
terms.net: Stanley Fish (Is There a Text in This Class?, 1980): shared interpretive strategies of a community that produce, rather than discover, the meaning of texts.

terms.hindi: स्त्री लेखिकाओं और उनकी परंपरा का अध्ययन।
terms.net: Elaine Showalter's term ('Towards a Feminist Poetics', 1979) for criticism concerned with woman as writer: female literary history, themes, genres and creativity.

terms.hindi: स्त्री के शरीर और अनुभव से निकली लेखन शैली।
terms.net: 'Feminine writing': Helene Cixous ('The Laugh of the Medusa', 1975); writing that inscribes the female body and difference, disrupting phallogocentric language.

terms.hindi: जिसे घिन या डर से अपने से दूर फेंक दिया जाए।
terms.net: Kristeva (Powers of Horror, 1980): the casting off of what threatens the boundary of the self (bodily waste, the corpse, the maternal).

terms.hindi: हर पाठ दूसरे पाठों से जुड़ा और बुना होता है।
terms.net: Term coined by Julia Kristeva ('Word, Dialogue and Novel', 1966/67) from Bakhtin's dialogism: every text is 'a mosaic of quotations', the absorption of another text.

terms.hindi: लिंग पहचान बार-बार किए गए व्यवहार से बनती है।
terms.net: Judith Butler (Gender Trouble, 1990): gender is not an essence but produced by repeated, stylized acts; drawn from Austin's speech-act theory.

terms.hindi: पश्चिम द्वारा पूरब की बनाई गई झूठी छवि।
terms.net: Edward Said (Orientalism, 1978): a Western discourse and 'style for dominating, restructuring, and having authority over the Orient'.

terms.hindi: समाज का दबा हुआ वर्ग जिसकी आवाज़ नहीं सुनी जाती।
terms.net: Gramsci's term for subordinated groups, used by Ranajit Guha's Subaltern Studies and Spivak ('Can the Subaltern Speak?', 1988).

terms.hindi: लड़ाई के लिए कुछ समय एक पहचान के नाम पर एकजुट होना।
terms.net: Spivak's term: the provisional, tactical adoption of an essential group identity for political ends, while knowing it is constructed.

terms.hindi: दो संस्कृतियों के मेल से बनी नई पहचान।
terms.net: Homi Bhabha (The Location of Culture, 1994): the mixing of coloniser and colonised cultures, which unsettles colonial authority's claim to purity.

terms.hindi: शासक की नकल जो पूरी कभी नहीं होती।
terms.net: Bhabha ('Of Mimicry and Man', 1984): the colonised subject as 'almost the same, but not quite', an ambivalence that both secures and menaces colonial power.

terms.hindi: शुद्ध अंग्रेज़ी के अधिकार को नकारना।
terms.net: Ashcroft, Griffiths and Tiffin (The Empire Writes Back, 1989): the rejection of a 'standard' English, followed by 'appropriation', its remoulding to new usages.

terms.hindi: किसी घटना का उसके पूरे सांस्कृतिक संदर्भ में विस्तार से वर्णन।
terms.net: Clifford Geertz (The Interpretation of Cultures, 1973), after Gilbert Ryle: description of behaviour along with its cultural meaning; adopted by New Historicists.

terms.hindi: साहित्य और प्रकृति-पर्यावरण के संबंध का अध्ययन।
terms.net: Term coined by William Rueckert (1978); defined by Cheryll Glotfelty (1996) as 'the study of the relationship between literature and the physical environment'.

terms.hindi: सब कुछ समझाने का दावा करने वाली बड़ी कहानी, जैसे प्रगति।
terms.net: Lyotard (The Postmodern Condition, 1979): grand narratives that legitimate knowledge (emancipation, progress, Hegelian spirit); postmodernism is 'incredulity toward' them.

terms.hindi: ऐसी नकल जिसका कोई असली मूल हो ही नहीं।
terms.net: Baudrillard (Simulacra and Simulation, 1981): a copy without an original; the final phase of the image, bearing no relation to any reality.

terms.hindi: नकली चीज़ें असली से भी ज़्यादा असली लगने लगें।
terms.net: Baudrillard's term for a condition in which simulations replace and precede the real, e.g. Disneyland, media images.

terms.hindi: इतिहास पर लिखा उपन्यास जो खुद पर भी सवाल उठाए।
terms.net: Linda Hutcheon (A Poetics of Postmodernism, 1988): self-reflexive novels that use historical events and figures while questioning how history is known and written.

terms.hindi: पुरानी शैलियों की बिना व्यंग्य की नकल।
terms.net: Imitation of styles; for Jameson (1984) the postmodern 'blank parody', a neutral mimicry lacking parody's satiric impulse.

terms.hindi: एक भाषा के भीतर कई सामाजिक बोलियाँ और आवाज़ें।
terms.net: Bakhtin ('Discourse in the Novel', 1934-35): the coexistence of diverse social languages and speech types within a language, orchestrated in the novel.

terms.hindi: उपन्यास में कई स्वतंत्र आवाज़ें, लेखक की आवाज़ हावी नहीं।
terms.net: Bakhtin (Problems of Dostoevsky's Poetics, 1929/1963): a plurality of independent, unmerged voices and consciousnesses, as in Dostoevsky.

terms.hindi: मेले जैसी उलट-पलट जहाँ ऊँच-नीच मिट जाए।
terms.net: Bakhtin (Rabelais and His World, 1965): literary mode drawn from folk carnival that subverts hierarchy through laughter, inversion and the grotesque body.

terms.hindi: कहानी में समय और स्थान का आपसी जुड़ाव।
terms.net: Bakhtin ('Forms of Time and of the Chronotope in the Novel', 1937-38): 'time-space', the intrinsic connectedness of temporal and spatial relationships in literature.

terms.hindi: पुरुषों के आपसी रिश्ते जो अक्सर स्त्री के ज़रिए बनते हैं।
terms.net: Sedgwick (Between Men, 1985): the continuum of male bonds, often routed through a woman in an 'erotic triangle'.

terms.hindi: यह मानना कि सिर्फ़ स्त्री-पुरुष संबंध ही सामान्य है।
terms.net: Term popularised by Michael Warner (Fear of a Queer Planet, 1991/1993): institutions and assumptions that make heterosexuality the norm.

mcqs.q: Who wrote 'Structure, Sign and Play in the Discourse of the Human Sciences'?
mcqs.exp: Derrida read it at Johns Hopkins in 1966.

mcqs.q: 'There is nothing outside the text' appears in:
mcqs.exp: Derrida's 'il n'y a pas de hors-texte' is from Of Grammatology (1967).

mcqs.q: Match the critics with their works: (a) Iser (b) Fish (c) Jauss (d) Rosenblatt -- (i) Is There a Text in This Class? (ii) The Act of Reading (iii) The Reader, the Text, the Poem (iv) Toward an Aesthetic of Reception
mcqs.exp: Iser: Act of Reading; Fish: interpretive communities; Jauss: reception aesthetics; Rosenblatt: transactional theory.

mcqs.q: Arrange in chronological order: (i) Orientalism (ii) The Second Sex (iii) Gender Trouble (iv) Of Grammatology
'Incredulity toward metanarratives' is Lyotard's definition of:
mcqs.exp: The Postmodern Condition (1979).

mcqs.q: Who coined the term 'historiographic metafiction'?
mcqs.exp: A Poetics of Postmodernism (1988).

mcqs.q: Which of the following is NOT one of the five codes in Barthes's S/Z?
mcqs.exp: The codes are hermeneutic, proairetic, semic, symbolic and cultural.

mcqs.q: The phrase 'Always historicize!' opens:
mcqs.exp: Jameson, The Political Unconscious (1981).

mcqs.q: Pierre Macherey's A Theory of Literary Production emphasises:
options: The organic unity of the text
The 'not-said' and silences of the text
mcqs.exp: Macherey reads gaps and absences produced by ideology.

mcqs.q: Assertion (A): For Lacan the unconscious is structured like a language. Reason (R): Lacan reinterpreted Freudian condensation and displacement as metaphor and metonymy.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
mcqs.exp: Lacan's linguistic reading of dream-work explains his claim.

mcqs.q: The 'mirror stage' is associated with:
mcqs.exp: Lacan's paper of 1936/1949, reprinted in Ecrits.

mcqs.q: Elaine Showalter's three phases of women's writing in A Literature of Their Own are:
mcqs.exp: Feminine (1840-80), Feminist (1880-1920), Female (1920-).

mcqs.q: The Madwoman in the Attic was written by:
mcqs.exp: Published 1979; title from Bertha Mason in Jane Eyre.

mcqs.q: 'One is not born, but rather becomes, a woman' was written by:
mcqs.exp: The Second Sex (1949).

mcqs.q: 'The Laugh of the Medusa' and ecriture feminine are associated with:
mcqs.exp: Cixous, 1975.

mcqs.q: Match: (a) Kristeva (b) Irigaray (c) Butler (d) Cixous -- (i) This Sex Which Is Not One (ii) Powers of Horror (iii) The Newly Born Woman (iv) Bodies That Matter
mcqs.exp: Kristeva: abjection; Irigaray: 1977; Butler: 1993; Cixous with Clement: 1975.

mcqs.q: Who coined the term 'intertextuality'?
mcqs.exp: Kristeva in 'Word, Dialogue and Novel', drawing on Bakhtin.

mcqs.q: 'Can the Subaltern Speak?' was written by:
Colonial mimicry as 'almost the same, but not quite' is a concept of:
mcqs.exp: Bhabha, 'Of Mimicry and Man' (1984), in The Location of Culture.

mcqs.q: 'Contrapuntal reading' is proposed by Edward Said in:
options: The World, the Text, and the Critic
mcqs.exp: Culture and Imperialism (1993), e.g. reading Mansfield Park.

mcqs.q: Match: (a) Fanon (b) Ngugi (c) Said (d) Ashcroft et al. -- (i) Decolonising the Mind (ii) The Empire Writes Back (iii) The Wretched of the Earth (iv) Orientalism
mcqs.exp: Fanon 1961; Ngugi 1986; Said 1978; Ashcroft, Griffiths, Tiffin 1989.

mcqs.q: The term 'New Historicism' was coined by:
mcqs.exp: Greenblatt in 1982; he later preferred 'cultural poetics'.

mcqs.q: Political Shakespeare (1985), the key text of Cultural Materialism, was edited by:
mcqs.exp: Jonathan Dollimore and Alan Sinfield.

mcqs.q: The term 'ecocriticism' was first used by:
mcqs.exp: Rueckert, 'Literature and Ecology: An Experiment in Ecocriticism' (1978).

mcqs.q: Which of the following is associated with Jean Baudrillard?
mcqs.exp: Simulacra and Simulation (1981); paralogy is Lyotard, rhizome Deleuze-Guattari, cognitive mapping Jameson.

mcqs.q: Which concept is NOT associated with Mikhail Bakhtin?
mcqs.exp: Differance is Derrida's.

mcqs.q: Who wrote Epistemology of the Closet (1990)?
mcqs.exp: Sedgwick; she also wrote Between Men (1985).

mcqs.q: 'Horizon of expectations' is a key concept of:
mcqs.exp: Jauss, Konstanz lecture of 1967.

mcqs.q: Discipline and Punish uses which model of surveillance?
mcqs.exp: Foucault (1975) took the Panopticon from Jeremy Bentham.

mcqs.q: Assertion (A): Althusser argues that ideology interpellates individuals as subjects. Reason (R): For Althusser, ideology works only through the Repressive State Apparatus such as police and army.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
mcqs.exp: Ideology works chiefly through Ideological State Apparatuses (school, church, family), not the RSA.
